meta.title: Multi-Agent Work Flow for Automated MBSE Model Generation: A Satellite System Case Study

abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering is essential for managing the complexity of modern aerospace systems, yet the transition from natural language requirements to formal system models remains a labor-intensive bottleneck. This paper presents a novel multi-agent framework leveraging Large Language Models to automate the generation of Systems Modeling Language models. The proposed architecture decomposes the modeling process into three specialized agents: a Requirement Analyzer that structures informal text, an XML Generator that synthesizes core model artifacts, and an XML Validator that ensures syntactic correctness through iterative self-correction. We validate this approach through both a quantitative comparative experiment and a communication satellite design case study, demonstrating the system’s ability to reliably generate compliant XMI files importable into tools like MagicDraw. The results suggest that multi-agent collaboration significantly improves the reliability and structural validity of code-based model generation compared to direct LLM inference.

blocks.html: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) promotes the use of formal, coherent models as the primary artifacts across the lifecycle of complex systems, replacing traditional document-centric approaches [1, 2]. Industrial MBSE tools, such as Cameo Systems Modeler/MagicDraw, support standardized modeling languages like SysML and enable model interchange via the XML Metadata Interchange (XMI) format. However, constructing such models is still largely a manual activity requiring deep domain expertise and familiarity with strict modeling syntax.

In the aerospace sector, early-phase requirements are predominantly communicated in natural language, such as stakeholder needs documents or conceptual design reports. Translating these informal descriptions into consistent SysML models is costly and often becomes a significant bottleneck. This challenge is especially evident in space systems (e.g., satellites and space probes), which involve multiple interacting subsystems—such as payload, power, thermal control, and attitude determination—and operate under strict Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) constraints. The intricate interdependencies among these subsystems make manual modeling prone to inconsistencies and omissions.

Concurrently, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have dramatically improved the ability to understand and generate structured content. LLM-based agents can now perform tasks such as requirement extraction, code generation, and complex reasoning with high degrees of fluency [3].

There is an increasing body of work on Artificial Intelligence for Systems Engineering (AI4SE) [4, 5]. Several studies explore the use of large language models to support requirement analysis or to map textual requirements to preliminary SysML requirement diagrams [6–8]. Recent efforts have also investigated the semi-automatic or agent-based generation of Capella or SysML models from textual use cases [9, 10].

However, most existing approaches suffer from significant limitations: they either remain at the proof-of-concept level, require substantial manual post-editing due to syntactic hallucinations, or lack a robust end-to-end pipeline from unstructured textual descriptions to executable structural models.

We address the problem of transforming a natural language description of a satellite mission into a fully compliant SysML structural model (in XMI format) that is directly importable into MagicDraw. This section introduces the system architecture built on a scalable orchestration engine and details the specific roles and mechanisms of the multi-agent algorithmic flow.

The implementation abstracts the LLM agents as operational nodes with directed edges encoding execution dependencies and data flow. The central orchestrator maintains and passes a shared state dictionary S = {r, y, x, m, f, k, s, p} across nodes. Here, k tracks the current repair iteration count, and s represents the execution status flag (e.g., success, need_revision).

As illustrated in Figure 1, the framework diverges from traditional single-prompt approaches by establishing a pipeline with an explicit feedback loop, enabling autonomous model verification and self-correction.
To efficiently map natural language to structured MBSE artifacts, the agents are designed with distinct responsibilities and tailored prompting strategies:

Requirement Analyzer (Areq): This agent reads the raw mission text r and invokes an LLM to output a YAML-formatted structure. Instead of letting the LLM freely summarize, we enforce a rigid schema. The agent extracts satellite_info (mission type, orbit), subsystems (components and logical ports), and critical requirements (mass, power). This formalizes the r 7→y step, acting as an information filter that guarantees a structured representation and drastically reduces downstream hallucination.

XML Generator (Agen): Taking the structured YAML y as the single source of truth, this agent prompts the LLM to generate the core UML XMI content (x). To overcome the LLM’s unfamiliarity with proprietary XMI structures, Agen utilizes few-shot prompting with an in-context SysML template. The template demonstrates how to construct a main satellite class, define subsystem composite properties (aggregation="composite"), and instantiate proxy ports. The prompt strictly enforces the generation of unique XMI IDs and localized element names.

XML Validator (Aval): Since LLMs (as autoregressive models) struggle to maintain long-range ID references perfectly, Aval acts as a deterministic gatekeeper. It wraps the generated fragment x into a complete XML document (adding necessary XMI headers and SysML profiles) and parses it using an XML validation script. If syntax errors (e.g., unclosed tags) or ID reference mismatches (e.g., a memberEnd pointing to a non-existent ID) are detected, Aval captures the exact error logs f and prompts the LLM to repair the specific fragment. This self-correction loop iterates until the model is completely valid or the maximum limit is reached.
The dynamic interaction and the iterative repair mechanism are governed by the orchestrator described in Algorithm 1.
To rigorously evaluate the proposed framework, we conducted both a quantitative comparison against a baseline method and a detailed qualitative case study in the context of space systems engineering.

We established a benchmark of 20 distinct satellite design textual prompts, varying in system complexity (ranging from simple 3-subsystem educational CubeSats to complex 8-subsystem low-earth orbit constellations). To rigorously account for the stochastic nature of LLM generation, each prompt was tested 5 times independently. This yielded a total of 100 evaluation trials for each method. We compared our Multi-Agent Workflow against a Single-Prompt LLM baseline, where the LLM is directly asked to generate the complete XMI model from the text in a zero-shot manner. All evaluation trials for both the baseline and our multi-agent framework were conducted using the locally deployed Qwen3-30B-A3B model.

The evaluation metrics include: Syntax Success Rate (percentage of the 100 generated models that pass basic XML tree parsing), Average Repair Iterations needed (applicable only to our method’s Validator), and MagicDraw Import Rate (percentage of the 100 models successfully imported as valid SysML Block Definition Diagrams without manual intervention).

As shown in Table 1, while the single-prompt baseline can generate parseable XML in nearly half of the trials (43.0%), it struggles significantly with the stringent SysML standards required by MBSE tools, ultimately producing a valid MagicDraw model in merely 7.0% of cases. Qualitative analysis of the baseline outputs reveals that although the general XML tree is intact, autoregressive models frequently hallucinate non-existent XMI attributes or mismatch xmi:idref pointers, which strictly prevents successful tool import.

Conversely, our multi-agent framework effectively bridges this semantic gap. Guided by the intermediate YAML schema and the Validator’s self-correction loop, the system guarantees a 100.0% syntactic success rate and an exceptional 98.0% tool-import rate. Notably, the system is highly efficient, requiring an average of only 1.4 repair iterations. This low iteration count indicates that the initial errors produced by the generator agent are typically minor and localized (e.g., isolated ID mismatches rather than complete structural failures). However, this rapid self-correction mechanism is highly crucial—it successfully targets and resolves these minor but fatal errors, transforming an otherwise broken generation process into a highly reliable and automated modeling workflow.

A specific test scenario involved designing a Ka-band communication satellite restricted to a mass of 500 kg and a 5-year mission life. The input text was written in unstructured natural language describing various operational needs.

The Requirement Analyzer successfully parsed the raw text into a YAML structure, accurately extracting functional subsystems. As reflected in the generated model, the system successfully identified core components such as the Communication Payload (with proxy ports like Data Input and RF Output) and the Data Transmission System (featuring Telemetry Data Output).

Following the generation phase, the Validator detected a minor idref mismatch in the attitude control subsystem’s association element. The error log was fed back to the Generator, which corrected the ID pointer in a single iteration. The final assembled XML was subsequently imported into MagicDraw. Figure 2 visualizes the successfully imported model within the MagicDraw Containment tree. The hierarchy flawlessly reflects the system composition, the explicitly defined PortKind interfaces, and the applied SysML profiles without any manual intervention, providing an immediate, structural starting point for systems engineers.

The proposed multi-agent pipeline significantly reduces the manual workload required in the early conceptual phases of aerospace design. By utilizing YAML as an intermediate state, the framework not only bridges the semantic gap between language and code but also encourages systematic system decomposition, which can subsequently support requirement traceability matrices. Furthermore, integrating the LLM into the validation loop enables autonomous self-repair of XML inconsistencies, replacing brittle rule-based scripts with robust, semantic correction. This marks a shift from "human-in-the-loop" authoring to "human-on-the-loop" supervision in MBSE.

blocks.html: Despite these advantages, limitations remain. The generation quality is still bounded by the LLM’s adherence to deep XML hierarchies, and extreme hallucinations in edge cases can occasionally disrupt the XMI structure beyond the Validator’s repair capability. Additionally, the current validation mechanism primarily checks syntactic correctness and reference integrity, rather than semantic physical consistency (e.g., verifying if the solar array power budget meets the payload demand). The output structure is also somewhat constrained by the initial SysML template, potentially limiting architectural diversity for highly unconventional spacecraft.

In conclusion, the primary contribution of our current work is the successful establishment and validation of this end-to-end automated workflow. While it provides a viable proof-of-concept from natural language to MBSE models, we are continuously refining the implementation details based on this methodology. Our ultimate goal is to push this framework towards a fully mature, industry-ready engineering solution for rapid space mission formulation. Future work will extend the framework to generate behavioral models (e.g., activity and state machine diagrams) and incorporate stronger semantic validation through integrations with domain-specific physics simulators or digital twin environments [5, 11, 12].
